prompt: A user with Windows Home wants to join the office Active Directory domain. What is the limitation?

options.text: Windows Home can join a domain if you turn on Bluetooth
Windows Home cannot join a domain; Windows Pro can
Only Windows Home can be a domain controller

explanation: Windows Home cannot join an Active Directory domain. Windows Pro, Enterprise, and Education can. Home also lacks Local Group Policy Editor and cannot host incoming Remote Desktop. If the job needs a domain logon, the PC needs an edition that supports it, not a setting buried in Home.

prompt: A user opens a file through a share. The share permission is Read. The NTFS permission is Full Control. What access do they get over the network?

options.text: Read, because the more restrictive of share and NTFS applies
Full Control, because NTFS always wins
No access, because the permissions disagree
Full Control, but only on Sundays

explanation: For a file opened over the network, Windows applies both the share permission and the NTFS permission, and the more restrictive one wins. Here that is Read. If the same user sits at the PC and opens the file locally, only NTFS applies, so local access could be Full Control. Check both lists when a share "looks right" but still blocks someone.

prompt: Windows system files look damaged. Which command scans and repairs protected system files?
explanation: sfc /scannow runs System File Checker, which compares protected Windows files with the store and repairs ones it can. Run it from an elevated prompt. If it cannot repair a file, DISM can restore the component store, and then you run SFC again. diskpart clean erases a disk. It is not a repair.

prompt: A volume has file-system errors and folders that will not open. Which Windows tool checks the disk?
explanation: chkdsk checks a volume for file-system problems. chkdsk /f fixes logical errors, and chkdsk /r also scans for bad sectors, which takes longer. It may need to run at the next boot if the volume is in use. It cannot revive a drive that is mechanically failing, so back up first if the files matter.

prompt: You changed a Group Policy setting and the PC has not picked it up. Which command refreshes policy now?

options.text: msinfo32 only shows it and does not refresh it

explanation: gpupdate refreshes Group Policy. gpupdate /force reapplies settings even if they do not look new. gpresult /r shows which policies actually applied and is the tool to use when a setting "should be there" but is not. A reboot also refreshes policy, but you do not have to wait for one.

prompt: A Mac user wants automatic backups of the home folder to an external disk. Which built-in feature is that?
explanation: Time Machine is the macOS backup tool. It copies files to a destination disk and lets you restore older versions. Spotlight is the Mac search feature, Mission Control shows spaces and windows, and Keychain Access stores passwords and certificates. File History is a Windows feature, not the Mac one.

prompt: On Linux, a normal user must run one installer command with elevated rights. What is the usual way?
explanation: sudo runs that one command with elevated privileges if the account is allowed to. It is not a reason to log in as root for the whole day. The user still needs to be in the sudoers policy. If sudo asks for a password, it wants that user password, not a second secret, on a typical setup.

prompt: You need to change who owns a file on Linux, not the read and write bits. Which command is that?
explanation: chown changes the owner and can change the group. chmod changes the permission bits, such as who can read or execute. People mix them up because both start with "ch." grep searches file contents, and pwd prints the current directory. Ownership and permission are two different columns when you run ls -l.

prompt: On a Debian-based Linux PC, which command refreshes the list of available packages without installing them yet?
explanation: apt update downloads the current package lists. apt upgrade installs the updates those lists describe. You usually run update first, then upgrade. chmod 777 makes a file writable by everyone and is not a package command. Do not use it to "fix" a permission error you have not read.

prompt: You want to find lines that contain the word "error" inside a log file. Which Linux command is the right kind of tool?

options.text: find, because it searches inside file contents

explanation: grep searches the contents of files and prints matching lines. find searches for files and directories by name, size, or time. Use find to locate the log, then grep to look inside it. ipconfig is a Windows command. The Linux equivalent for addresses is ip or ifconfig.

prompt: You are installing Windows on a 4 TB disk in UEFI mode. Which partition table belongs on that disk?

options.text: MBR, because it allows disks larger than 2 TB

explanation: GPT is the partition table used with UEFI and it supports large disks. MBR is the legacy table, with a roughly 2 TB limit and only four primary partitions. The Windows installer in UEFI mode will create a GPT disk. Mixing a legacy BIOS boot with GPT, or UEFI with MBR, is a common reason a new install will not boot.

prompt: Windows will not finish booting after a driver install. You want to start with a minimal set of drivers. Which mode is that?
explanation: Safe Mode loads a minimal set of drivers and services. Use it when a bad driver, startup app, or piece of malware blocks a normal boot. From there you can roll back a driver or run a scan. It is not a permanent way to run the PC, and some devices will not work until you boot normally again.

prompt: Which statement about a 64-bit version of Windows is accurate?

options.text: It can run 32-bit apps and address much more than 4 GB of RAM
It only runs on ARM tablets from 2012
It removes the need for user accounts

explanation: A 64-bit Windows install can run 32-bit applications and can use far more than 4 GB of RAM when the hardware has it. A 32-bit Windows install cannot run 64-bit applications and is limited to about 4 GB of RAM. Match the edition and the drivers to the bitness. A 64-bit printer driver will not load on a 32-bit OS.

prompt: A user asks where "Finder" is on their Windows 11 PC. What do you tell them?

options.text: Finder is the Windows file manager
Finder is the name of Task Manager
Windows uses File Explorer; Finder is the macOS file manager
Finder was replaced by the BIOS

explanation: File Explorer is the Windows file manager. Finder is the macOS one. The jobs are similar, so users mix the names up. On Windows, Win+E opens File Explorer. On a Mac, Finder is the smiling face in the Dock. Using the right name in a ticket keeps the next technician from looking for a menu that is not there.

prompt: A Windows Home laptop needs full-volume BitLocker with the usual management tools. What is the catch?

options.text: BitLocker is a Pro feature and is not the Home edition toolset
BitLocker replaces the need for a password

explanation: BitLocker is available on Windows Pro, Enterprise, and Education. Windows Home may offer a simpler device encryption on some hardware, but it is not the same management experience. BitLocker encrypts the volume so a stolen drive is not readable in another PC. It does not replace a sign-in password or a backup.

prompt: Which Windows tools help you check startup programs and system logs? Select all that apply.
explanation: Task Manager has a Startup tab that shows what launches at sign-in, and it shows CPU, memory, and disk use. Event Viewer holds the Windows logs, including application crashes and service failures. Time Machine and Finder are macOS tools. They will not be on a Windows PC unless someone is describing the wrong operating system.

prompt: A change request describes the new mail setting but not how to undo it if mail stops flowing. What is missing?
explanation: A backout plan is the written way to return to the last working state if the change fails. You want it before you start, not after the outage. The rest of a solid request includes the purpose, the scope, the risk, who approved it, and how the user will accept the result. Hope is not a backout plan.

prompt: A weekend change is finished. Who should confirm that the business process actually works again?

options.text: Only the technician who made the change
The affected user or business owner, as end-user acceptance
Nobody, if the lights are on

explanation: End-user acceptance means the person who depends on the system confirms the change did what they needed. The technician can prove a service is running and still miss the real workflow. Schedule that check, especially after a weekend change, and write the answer in the ticket before you call the change closed.

prompt: Which backup type copies only what changed since the last backup of any type?

options.text: A RAID 1 mirror in the same PC

explanation: An incremental backup copies changes since the last backup, whether that last one was full or incremental. A differential copies everything since the last full backup, so it grows until the next full. Restoring incrementals needs the full backup plus every incremental since it, in order. A mirror in the same PC is not a backup.

prompt: Backups run every night and have never been restored. What is the gap?

options.text: The wallpaper is backed up twice
A backup you have not successfully restored is unverified

explanation: The only proof of a backup is a restore. Test restores on a schedule and after you change backup software. A job that "completed" can still hold corrupt files or skip the folder the user cares about. Write down how long the restore took so the team knows whether it fits the time they can be down.

prompt: Which statement matches the 3-2-1 backup idea?

options.text: Three passwords, two monitors, one printer
Three copies of the data, on two kinds of media, with one copy offsite
Three RAID 0 arrays in the same rack

explanation: 3-2-1 means three copies, two different media types, and one copy kept offsite so a fire or theft does not take everything. The production files count as one copy. A second disk in the same PC is not the offsite copy. Cloud storage can be the offsite copy if the account is protected and you have tested a restore.

prompt: When is an anti-static wrist strap the right tool, and when should it come off?

options.text: Wear it while handling boards; take it off before you work inside a power supply or on a CRT
Wear it while the power supply is open and powered
Never wear it; carpets are safer
Wear it only when using a degausser on an SSD

explanation: A wrist strap keeps you and the PC at the same potential so a static discharge does not punch a hole in a chip. Bond it to ground, and unplug the PC before you work inside. Do not wear the strap while you service high-voltage parts such as a power-supply interior or an old CRT. Those can still hold a dangerous charge.

prompt: A desktop power supply is buzzing and smells hot. A coworker wants to open the supply case with the strap on. What do you say?

options.text: Open it and measure the capacitors by hand
Wash it with water while it is plugged in
Do not open a power supply; replace it

explanation: Power supplies store a dangerous charge even after they are unplugged, and they are not a field-repair part. Replace the supply with one of the right wattage and connectors. Do not open the case, and do not keep running a supply that smells hot. The same "do not open" rule applies to old CRT monitors.

prompt: Toner spilled on a desk. Where do you look for the safe cleanup method?
explanation: The safety data sheet (SDS), formerly called an MSDS, describes the chemical, the hazards, and how to clean it up. Toner is a fine powder. A normal household vacuum can blow it into the air and the dust can be a fire hazard in the vacuum. Use a toner-rated vacuum or the method the SDS lists, and wash skin with cold water rather than hot.

prompt: The office wants the phone system to stay up during a short power cut. A surge strip is already installed. What else is required?

options.text: Another surge strip daisy-chained to the first
A UPS, because a surge strip does not provide battery power

explanation: A surge protector clamps voltage spikes. It does nothing when the power goes out. A UPS has a battery and can keep the phones or a server running long enough for a clean shutdown or for a generator to start. Do not daisy-chain surge strips. Size the UPS for the load and test it, because batteries age out.

prompt: A ticket about a payroll problem includes an employee full name and social security number. How should that data be handled?

options.text: It is PII and does not belong in a casual screenshot or a personal USB drive
Post it in the public lobby so the user can see it
Email it to your personal account to work from home more easily
It is not sensitive because it is already on a computer

explanation: A name plus a social security number is personally identifiable information. Put only what the ticket system is approved to hold, lock the screen when you walk away, and do not copy it to a personal drive or a home email account. If the data was exposed, tell your supervisor so the company can follow its incident process.

prompt: You arrive at a user desk to fix a PC. What is the professional way to start?

options.text: Move their chair and start clicking without a word
Read their open email out loud so you understand the job
Introduce yourself, ask permission, and explain what you are going to do in plain language
Tell them the problem is obvious and they should already know

explanation: Ask before you touch someone else computer, and say what you are about to do without unnecessary jargon. If you must use a technical word, explain it. Do not browse files that are not part of the problem, and do not make the user feel foolish for calling. The way you start the visit is part of the support, not a delay in front of it.

prompt: What belongs in the ticket when you close a problem?

options.text: The symptom, the steps you tried, and how you confirmed the resolution

explanation: The next technician should be able to see the symptom, what you changed, and how you knew it worked. "Fixed" leaves them guessing. Leave out personal comments and any data the ticket does not need. If you promised a follow-up, write the date. Good notes are how a help desk gets faster without rushing the person in front of you.

prompt: Which file extension is a PowerShell script?
explanation: PowerShell scripts use .ps1. Batch files use .bat, and a Linux shell script often uses .sh. Python uses .py, and JavaScript uses .js. You run the script with the right interpreter, and you do not bypass execution policy on a work PC just to "see if it works." A .jpg is a picture, not a script.

prompt: A remote site wants command-line access to a router. Which protocol should they use?

options.text: HTTP on port 80 with the admin password

explanation: SSH encrypts remote command-line administration. Telnet sends keystrokes, including passwords, in the clear. HTTP admin pages have the same problem unless they are HTTPS. An open mail relay is unrelated and is something you close, not a management tool. If the only option today is Telnet, use it inside a VPN and plan to turn it off.

prompt: A technician needs to see and control a Windows desktop at another site. Which tool matches that job?

options.text: Remote Desktop, preferably reached through a VPN rather than an open port 3389

explanation: Remote Desktop Protocol gives a graphical Windows session. The server listens on TCP 3389 by default. Leaving that port open to the internet invites password guessing, so reach it through a VPN or a remote gateway. ping only tests reachability. A toner probe traces a cable. chkdsk checks a disk.

prompt: Which items belong in a change request? Select all that apply.

options.text: Copies of the user personal photos
A joke to keep the meeting short

explanation: Scope says what will change and what will not. A backout plan says how you undo it. The request should also cover why, the risk, the timing, and who approved it. Personal photos and jokes do not belong in the record. A clear request is what lets someone else support the change at 2 a.m.

prompt: A coworker copies one retail Windows license onto a second PC to save money. Why is that a problem?

options.text: Retail licenses can be pasted onto as many PCs as you want
The second install is fine if both PCs are the same color
One license does not automatically cover two installs; the EULA decides how it can be used

explanation: The end-user license agreement says how many installs the license allows. One retail license is not a free pass for a second PC, and an OEM license is usually tied to the device it came with. Unlicensed software is a policy and legal problem, not a clever shortcut. When in doubt, check the agreement or ask the person who owns licensing.

prompt: A building entrance has two doors with a small room between them, and the second door will not open until the first door closes. What is that control?
explanation: An access control vestibule is a two-door entry that holds a person between doors so staff can confirm who they are. Older notes call this a mantrap. A bollard is a post that stops a vehicle. A cable lock secures a laptop chassis. A privacy filter narrows a screen viewing angle.

prompt: A stranger follows you through the badge door without badging, and you did not invite them. What is that called?
explanation: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a door without permission. Piggybacking is the related case where the authorized person knowingly holds the door. Both skip the badge check. The polite response is to send the person back to the desk, not to hold the door because it feels rude to refuse.

prompt: A login requires a password and a fingerprint. Which factors are those?

options.text: Something you know and something you are
Two copies of something you know
A biometric and another biometric only

explanation: A password is something you know. A fingerprint is something you are. Using both is multi-factor authentication. A phone authenticator app or a hardware token is something you have. Two passwords are still one factor, just asked twice. MFA is stronger because stealing one factor is not enough.

prompt: Help-desk accounts are all members of Domain Admins so tickets get closed faster. What principle does that break?
explanation: Least privilege means an account gets only the access the job needs. A help-desk tech who can reset passwords does not need to own the domain. Extra admin rights turn one phished mailbox into a forest-wide incident. Give the specific rights the procedure needs, and use a separate admin account for those moments.

prompt: A caller claims to be from the bank and asks a user to read back a one-time code. The user did not start this call. What kind of attack is that?

options.text: A brute-force attack on the badge reader

explanation: Vishing is phishing by voice. Smishing is the same trick over text messages. Email phishing uses a message and a link. The user should hang up and call the bank on a number from the card or the official site, not a number the caller gives. A one-time code is as good as a password once it is read aloud.

prompt: A wireless network appears with the same name as the company SSID, but it is not one of your access points. What is that?
explanation: An evil twin is a rogue access point using a trusted SSID so clients connect and the attacker can watch traffic. Users should use the company wireless profile, and guests should use the guest network. Hiding the real SSID does not stop this. 802.1X with certificates makes the fake access point much harder to impersonate.

prompt: Why should WPS be turned off on a small-office wireless router?

options.text: WPS is required for WPA3 and must stay on
WPS makes the 5 GHz band illegal
The WPS PIN method is weak and is often left open to guessing
WPS disables the DHCP server permanently

explanation: Wi-Fi Protected Setup was meant to make joining easy, especially with a PIN. That PIN can be guessed, so an attacker can learn the Wi-Fi password. Turn WPS off and give users the WPA2 or WPA3 passphrase through a normal channel. A push-button is more convenient than a PIN, and it is still something you disable when you do not need it.

prompt: A PC shows a note that files are encrypted and payment will unlock them. What is the best first response?

options.text: Pay immediately from the company card
Disconnect the PC from the network and start the incident process, including a clean backup
Email the note to the whole company as a joke
Run Disk Cleanup and ignore it

explanation: This is ransomware. Isolate the PC so it cannot encrypt mapped drives and other PCs. Do not pay as the first plan. Payment does not guarantee a key, and it marks the company as a target. Restore from a backup that was not online and reachable by the malware, and follow the company incident process.

prompt: You need to destroy data on an SSD before the drive is retired. Why is degaussing the wrong tool?

options.text: Degaussing will make the SSD faster
SSDs are already encrypted by VGA
Degaussing erases magnetic media, and an SSD does not store data that way

explanation: A degausser scrambles magnetic domains, so it can destroy hard disks and tapes. An SSD stores charge in flash cells, so a magnet does not erase it. Use the vendor secure-erase command, crypto-erase if the drive was encrypted, or physical destruction. A quick format only removes the pointers and leaves the data recoverable.

prompt: A user wants one spreadsheet encrypted, not the whole drive. Which Windows feature matches that request?
explanation: Encrypting File System (EFS) encrypts individual files and folders and is tied to the user certificate. BitLocker encrypts the volume, which protects a stolen disk even if someone moves it to another PC. They solve different problems. EFS will not help if the user account is compromised, because Windows decrypts the file for that user when they sign in.

prompt: People walking behind a user can read the password as it is typed. What is the attack, and what physical control helps?

options.text: Smishing, stopped by a toner vacuum
Shoulder surfing, reduced by a privacy filter and by sitting with the screen out of the aisle
An evil twin, stopped by a cable lock

explanation: Shoulder surfing is watching a screen or a keypad. A privacy filter narrows the angle where the picture is visible, and desk placement matters too. It does not encrypt anything. Teach users to cover a PIN pad. A cable lock stops theft of the laptop, not someone reading over a shoulder.

prompt: Attackers are using a flaw that the software vendor has not patched yet. What is that flaw called?
explanation: A zero-day is a vulnerability that is being exploited before the vendor has a patch, so there have been zero days of a fix. You reduce damage with least privilege, network limits, and detection, then patch as soon as a fix exists. End-of-life software never gets that fix, which is why it should leave the network.

prompt: A program asks Windows for administrator rights and a dimmed prompt appears. What is that prompt?

options.text: The BIOS splash that cannot be skipped

explanation: User Account Control (UAC) asks for approval before a program makes an administrative change. Users should read it, not click Yes out of habit. It is not a virus scan. If a prompt appears when they did not launch anything, they should cancel and tell the help desk. Turning UAC off removes that pause.

prompt: A user wants to block unsolicited inbound connections on a Windows laptop. Which control does that job?
explanation: A firewall filters network traffic and can block inbound connections the PC did not ask for. Antivirus scans files and programs for malware. They are different tools, and Windows includes both. A firewall does not decide whether a downloaded installer is trustworthy. That is the scanner and the user decision.

prompt: A drive may be evidence in an investigation. What record shows who had it, and when, from collection through storage?
explanation: Chain of custody is the written history of evidence: who collected it, who held it, when it moved, and where it was stored. Gaps make the evidence easier to challenge. Do not power a suspect drive on and browse it. Follow the company process, label it, and keep the log with the item.

prompt: Which of these are physical security controls? Select all that apply.
explanation: A badge reader and bollards are physical controls. The reader decides who can open a door, and bollards stop a vehicle from reaching the door. WPA3 is wireless encryption, and an email filter is a logical control on messages. Physical and logical controls stack. Neither one replaces the other.

prompt: You have confirmed that a Windows PC is running malware. What is the next step in the best-practice removal process?

options.text: Educate the user, then leave it on the network
Quarantine the system by disconnecting it from the network
Pay the popup so the scan can finish

explanation: After you verify the symptoms, quarantine the PC so it cannot spread or keep talking to an attacker. Then, on Windows, disable System Restore, remediate with updated tools and scans, schedule later scans and updates, turn System Restore back on with a new restore point, and educate the user. Paying a popup is not a step.

prompt: Why do you disable System Restore before removing malware from Windows?

options.text: System Restore is what encrypted the files
Old restore points can contain the malware and reinfect the PC
System Restore blocks all network cables physically

explanation: Restore points can store the infection. If someone rolls back after a cleanup, the malware returns. Disable System Restore before the cleanup, then enable it again and create a fresh restore point once the system is clean. This step is specific to Windows. The rest of the removal order still applies.

prompt: What is the last step in the malware removal best-practice process?

options.text: Disable System Restore and leave it off forever
Hide the incident from the user

explanation: The last step is teaching the user how the infection happened and how to avoid the next one. Before that, you schedule scans and updates, and on Windows you turn System Restore back on. A cleanup that the user does not understand gets repeated. Keep the lesson specific: which attachment, which prompt, which site.

prompt: Windows hits a blue stop screen after a driver update. What is the most useful first note to take?

options.text: The stop code, and what changed just before it
The user favorite browser homepage only

explanation: The stop code and the recent change point at the driver or update to roll back. A photo of the screen is better than a paraphrase. Then use Safe Mode, recovery, or the vendor rollback. Reinstalling Windows is a late option after you have saved the user files and tried the obvious reversal.

prompt: A browser opens extra pages the user did not click, and a new toolbar appeared overnight. What kind of problem is that?

options.text: A malware symptom, often adware or a browser hijacker

explanation: Unwanted toolbars, a changed homepage, and redirects are classic adware or hijacker symptoms. Remove the unknown extension, scan with updated anti-malware, and check the other browsers too. Do not click the popup that offers to clean the PC for a fee. That popup is often part of the same problem.

prompt: A PC is slow from the moment the user signs in. Task Manager shows many apps at startup and the disk is 98 percent full. What should you address first?

options.text: Replace the CPU before you look at software
Free disk space and disable unneeded startup apps

explanation: A full disk and a crowd of startup programs will make sign-in feel broken without any hardware failure. Clear space, then turn off startup items the user does not need. If it is still slow, look at malware and at which process is using the disk. Replacing the CPU does not fix a drive that has no room left.

prompt: A PC says "no boot device found." The drive was working yesterday. Which checks come first?

options.text: Whether the drive is detected, the boot order, and loose SATA or power cables

explanation: Start with detection and boot order. A USB stick left ahead of the hard drive, a loose SATA cable, or a drive that no longer appears in firmware all produce this message. If the drive is missing in firmware, suspect the cable, power, or the drive itself. Reinstalling Windows will not help a disk the firmware cannot see.

prompt: A phone will not install an app update and warns that storage is full. What is the right first fix?

options.text: Factory reset before you look at storage
Free space by removing files or unused apps, then retry the update

explanation: Updates need free space for the download and the unpack. Delete files the user can live without, or move photos off the phone, then try again. A factory reset erases the device and is a last step after a backup, not the first response to a full disk. Degaussing is not a phone repair.

prompt: One mobile app closes as soon as it opens. Other apps work. What should you try before a factory reset?

options.text: Update or reinstall that app, restart, and clear its cache
Disable the firewall on every PC in the office

explanation: One crashing app is usually that app, not the whole phone. Update it, restart the phone, and clear its cache. Reinstall if the cache clear is not enough. Back up before any reset that erases data. Wiping the phone to fix one app throws away contacts and photos the user may not have copied.

prompt: A full-screen page says the PC is infected and lists a phone number to call for a paid cleaner. The user did not install a scanner. What is this?

options.text: Scareware, and they should close it without calling or paying
A Windows update that must be paid in gift cards
The official System File Checker window

explanation: Scareware imitates a security alert and pushes a payment or a phone call. Close the page, do not call, and do not download the offered cleaner. Then scan with a tool the company already trusts. Gift-card payments are a second sign that the message is a scam. Real Windows tools do not demand a prepaid card.

prompt: One Windows profile loads to a black desktop and crashes. A new profile on the same PC works. What does that pattern suggest?

options.text: The power supply is too efficient
The monitor cable is VGA, so profiles cannot load
The RAM is ECC and refuses that user
The user profile is corrupt, and data may need to be copied to a new profile

explanation: If a new account works and the old one does not, the Windows install is mostly fine and that profile is the problem. Create a new profile, copy documents from the old profile folder, and leave the broken one until the copy is checked. Reinstalling Windows is unnecessary when a second account already proves the system boots.

prompt: A Windows service is set to start automatically, but it stops within a few seconds. Where do you look first?

options.text: Event Viewer, the service dependencies, and the account the service uses to sign in
The plenum rating of the patch cable

explanation: Event Viewer usually has an error from the service or from Service Control Manager. Then check that required services are running and that the logon account is not locked or using a wrong password. Starting it again without reading the error just repeats the failure. The cable jacket and the monitor cable do not stop a service.

prompt: Users cannot sign in, and browsers warn that certificates are not valid yet. The PCs show the year as 2019. What should you correct?

options.text: The date and time, then confirm they stay synced

explanation: Kerberos sign-in and TLS certificates depend on a clock that is close to the right time. A dead CMOS battery, a wrong time zone, or a blocked time server can all leave the clock years off. Set the time, find out why it drifted, and confirm it survives a reboot. Reinstalling the browser does not fix a clock.

prompt: Print jobs sit in the queue and nothing comes out. The printer itself is online. What is a reasonable Windows fix to try?

options.text: Restart the Print Spooler service and clear the stuck jobs
Disable the firewall on the domain controller forever
Convert the disk from GPT to MBR while the user is working

explanation: A stuck spooler holds jobs that the printer never sees. Restart the Print Spooler service and cancel the bad job. If jobs return as garbage, check the driver next. Do not reformat a disk or open Telnet because a queue is jammed. Also confirm the user is pointed at the right printer, not an offline duplicate.

prompt: Anti-malware removes a threat, and the same threat is back after a reboot. Scans from inside Windows do not stick. What is a reasonable next level of response?

options.text: Ignore it, because the scan count is high
Scan from a clean boot environment, or reimage from a known-good source
Give the malware local admin so it stops hiding

explanation: Malware that returns at boot, especially a rootkit, can load before the scanner. Boot a trusted scanner from clean media, or reimage the PC and restore data from a backup made before the infection. Giving it admin rights is the opposite of containment. After the rebuild, patch and change passwords that were typed on that PC.

prompt: Which of these are malware symptoms? Select all that apply.

options.text: The browser opens unfamiliar sites by itself
Security software is turned off and will not stay enabled

explanation: Redirects and security tools that will not stay on are signs the PC is being changed by software the user did not intend. A missing screw or a VGA cable can be real hardware notes, but they are not malware symptoms. Treat the software signs with the removal process: confirm, quarantine, clean, then teach the user what to watch for.
